title: Robbing behaviour and how to stop it
subtitle: Protecting hives when foragers from other colonies steal stored honey.
excerpt: Robbing happens when foragers from other hives discover an unguarded entrance and begin looting stored honey. It spreads fast: once robbers succeed they recruit more, and the attacked colony's defenders are overwhelmed within hours. Recognising the signs early and reducing the entrance in time stops the situation before it escalates.
sourceNotes: BBKA technical leaflet on robbing and washboarding (2021). NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit, section on hive security (2024). Frank Pearson, Bee-keeping for All (1923), Internet Archive, chapter on autumn management. Cornell Cooperative Extension, Managing Honey Bee Robbing (2019).

glossaryTerms.definition: When bees from other colonies force entry into a hive to steal stored honey, most common during the late-summer and autumn dearth when little nectar is available from flowers.
A period when no nectar is available in the field, typically from late July onward in the UK after the main summer flow ends.
A wooden or plastic strip that narrows the hive entrance to a small opening, making it easier for guard bees to defend against intruders.

content.text: Robbing

is one of the most damaging things that can happen to a hive in late summer and autumn. It begins when foragers from another colony find a gap in the defences and return home with stolen honey. Once they report back, the numbers escalate rapidly: a struggling colony can be under serious assault within the hour.
When robbing happens
Robbing is a feature of the
dearth

: the period after the summer flow ends, typically from late July in the UK, when little or no nectar comes in from the field. Bees from stronger colonies or feral nests start exploring, and a weak colony with a large entrance and few guard bees is exactly what they need.
Other common triggers: leaving supers or combs of honey uncovered outside the hive, feeding with the lid off, or disturbing a wasp nest near the apiary. Any exposed honey source invites attention.
Recognising the signs
More activity than usual at the entrance despite no obvious nectar flow outside.
Bees fighting on the landing board: grappling pairs tumbling off the edge.
Dead bees accumulating in front of the hive.
Bees investigating gaps and cracks in the hive body, not just the entrance.
Robber bees fly with a distinctly darting pattern and half-open wings as they approach. They leave heavy, struggling slightly to fly, abdomen full of stolen honey.
Immediate response
Fit an
entrance reducer

immediately. A mouse guard reduces the opening to a bee-width slot. If you have neither to hand, push a handful of fresh grass loosely across the entrance: robbers will not force through it but your colony can clear a path quickly.
Check every joint in the hive body for gaps. Unsealed cracks and a poorly seated crown board give robbers a side entrance your guard bees cannot cover.
Cover any exposed honey. Close rapid feeders, move uncovered supers indoors, clean up any syrup spilled during feeding.
Do not open the hive now. Lifting the crown board releases honey scent and removes the entrance as the single point your defenders are holding.
Keep the entrance reduced for at least three days after fighting visibly stops. Robbers return the following morning if they succeeded the day before.
If the assault is overwhelming

When fighting is heavy despite the reduced entrance, lay a damp sack flat across the landing board. The unusual substrate confuses robbers; your resident bees already know the hive by scent and work around it. Remove after 24 hours once
robbing
pressure eases.

A very weak or queenless colony that cannot defend even a reduced entrance may need uniting with a stronger colony before it loses all its stores. A colony that loses its honey reserves to robbing at this time of year will not survive winter.
Prevention
Reduce all hive entrances in late summer before the dearth bites, typically mid-August in most UK locations.
Never leave combs or supers uncovered outside the hive during a dearth. Even the faint honey smell in an empty super draws foragers.
Feed in the evening, when foraging activity is low. Wipe up any syrup spill and close the feeder fully before dark.
Keep colonies strong. A populous colony defends a small entrance very effectively. Weak colonies are the first attacked and the hardest to save once robbing starts.

attrs.cue: Fighting stops at night but restarts next morning
attrs.cause: Robbers are returning from the same source colony daily
attrs.fix: Keep the entrance reduced for a full week. Check for secondary cracks in the hive body that give side access.

attrs.cue: Cannot tell robbers from resident bees
attrs.fix: Watch bees leaving the attacked hive: robbers depart heavier and more slowly, abdomen visibly distended with stolen honey. Resident bees emerge normally.

attrs.cue: Entrance reducer does not stop the assault
attrs.cause: Colony may already have too few guard bees to hold even a narrow entrance
attrs.fix: Unite with a stronger colony using the newspaper method. A colony that cannot defend itself will be dead within days.
